Where it began

James Anderson, Jimmy to almost everyone, was born in Burnley on 30 July 1982. He grew up at Burnley Cricket Club, where as a boy he kept score for the second XI at weekends and in the school holidays. All he wanted was to be a cricketer. Around 17 he had a growth spurt and suddenly found real pace, and he was soon among the quickest bowlers in the Lancashire League.

In his first season of first-class cricket for Lancashire, 2002, he took 50 wickets in 13 matches and was named the county's most promising young player that season.

The player

England picked him for one-day cricket at 20, before Lancashire had even given him his cap. His Test debut came against Zimbabwe at Lord's in 2003, and he took five wickets in the first innings. The early years had their ups and downs, but by 2010 he led the England attack, and on the Ashes tour of 2010–11 he found a wobbling seam delivery to beat the Australian ball.

In 188 Tests between 2003 and 2024 he took 704 wickets at 26.46, with a best of 7 for 42 and 32 five-wicket hauls. He was the first fast bowler to reach 600 Test wickets and then 700, and by November 2026, on our figures, only one man had played more Tests and only two had taken more Test wickets. He had six spells at the top of the world Test bowling rankings and, in February 2023, became the oldest man ever to get there. He played his last Test in July 2024, by then Sir James Anderson.

What made him special

Swing was his craft, and he could move the ball both ways at a lively fast-medium. His action was famously odd: at the moment of release his head was down and his eyes closed. He tried bowling with his head up, lost pace, and went back to doing it his way.

Batting was another matter. His Test average was 8.96, yet he made 81 one day and shared a last-wicket stand of 198 with Joe Root, a world record. There was more in that bat than the average let on.

Away from the middle

He supports Burnley, and as a young man he worked part-time in the football club's ticket office. He designed clothes for a menswear label and later launched his own, and he became an OBE and a Wisden Cricketer of the Year. In 2018 the ECB named him in England's greatest Test XI. His autobiography, Finding The Edge, came out in 2024. In 2026, at 43, he captained Lancashire, took his 56th first-class five-wicket haul and finished as the club's leading wicket-taker with 50 wickets.

And finally

In 2003 one old England quick reckoned that unusual action might last five years. It lasted more than twenty, which may be the best argument yet for bowling with your eyes shut.
